questions.title: Pilus mediates bacterial adherence to mucous membranes
questions.question: The initial step in the process of many bacterial infections is adherence of the organism to mucous membranes. The bacterial component that mediates adherence is the?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Lipid A is the toxic component of lipopolysaccharide in the Gram-negative outer membrane; it triggers inflammatory/septic effects once infection is established, but it does not mediate the initial attachment step.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The nucleoid is the unbound cytoplasmic region holding the bacterial chromosome; it plays no role in surface adherence.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Peptidoglycan gives the cell wall its rigidity and shape; it is not the specific structure bacteria use to attach to host mucosal surfaces.
explanations.D: Correct. The (ordinary/common) pilus is a thin, protein (pilin) appendage on the bacterial surface specialised for adherence -- it is the structure that lets a bacterium first attach to mucosal epithelium, the essential first step before an organism can colonise and go on to cause infection. This adherence function is distinct from the sex pilus, a related but separate structure used for conjugation, and distinct from the flagellum, which drives motility rather than attachment. Losing this adherence step (e.g. by blocking pilus binding) is one strategy used to prevent infection before it starts.
explanations.E: Incorrect. A plasmid is extrachromosomal DNA carrying accessory genes (e.g. resistance genes); it is a genetic element, not a surface structure that mediates attachment.

questions.learning_objective: State that the (ordinary) pilus mediates bacterial adherence to mucosal epithelium, the first step in many infections, distinguishing it from the sex pilus, flagellum and other surface structures.

questions.title: Thick vs thin peptidoglycan is the true gram-positive/negative wall difference
questions.question: Which one of the following is the most accurate description of the structural differences between gram-positive bacteria and gram-negative bacteria?

options.A: Gram-positive bacteria have a thick peptidoglycan layer whereas gram-negative bacteria have a thin layer
options.B: Gram-positive bacteria have an outer lipid-rich membrane whereas gram-negative bacteria do not
options.C: Gram-positive bacteria form a sex pilus that mediates conjugation whereas gram-negative bacteria do not
options.D: Gram-positive bacteria have plasmids whereas gram-negative bacteria do not
options.E: Gram-positive bacteria have capsules whereas gram-negative bacteria do not

explanations.A: Correct. The most accurate structural distinction between the two groups is peptidoglycan thickness: Gram-positive bacteria have a thick, multilayered peptidoglycan wall that retains the crystal violet stain, while Gram-negative bacteria have only a thin peptidoglycan layer sandwiched beneath an outer lipid membrane. This thickness difference is the direct mechanistic basis of the Gram stain result itself, and it also explains why Gram-positive walls can carry teichoic acid within their thick mesh while Gram-negative walls cannot. None of the other listed features (outer membrane presence, sex pilus, plasmids, capsules) actually differs systematically by Gram type the way peptidoglycan thickness does.
explanations.B: Incorrect. This reverses the truth -- it is Gram-negative bacteria that have the outer lipid-rich membrane (carrying LPS), not Gram-positive bacteria, which lack an outer membrane entirely.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The sex pilus, used for conjugative DNA transfer, is not restricted to Gram-positive bacteria -- conjugation occurs in both Gram-positive and Gram-negative organisms, and it is unrelated to the cell-wall structural difference the question is asking about.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Plasmids (extrachromosomal DNA) occur in both Gram-positive and Gram-negative bacteria; carrying plasmids is not a distinguishing wall-structure feature.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Capsules are found in both Gram-positive and Gram-negative species (e.g. pneumococcus is Gram-positive and encapsulated, while Klebsiella is Gram-negative and encapsulated); capsule presence does not track with Gram type.

questions.learning_objective: Identify peptidoglycan thickness (thick in Gram-positive, thin in Gram-negative) as the accurate structural difference between the two wall types, rejecting outer-membrane, sex-pilus, plasmid and capsule distractors that do not track with Gram type.

questions.title: Bacterial flagella are antigenic, not shared with human structures
questions.question: Each of the following statements concerning the surface structures of bacteria is correct EXCEPT?

options.A: Pili mediate the interaction of bacteria with mucosal epithelium
options.C: Both gram-negative rods and cocci have lipopolysaccharide endotoxin in their cell wall
options.D: Bacterial flagella are nonantigenic in humans because they closely resemble human flagella in chemical composition

explanations.A: Incorrect (this is a true statement, so it is not the EXCEPT answer). Pili do mediate bacterial interaction with (adherence to) mucosal epithelium, the first step in establishing many infections.
explanations.B: Incorrect (true statement). Polysaccharide capsules genuinely retard phagocytosis, a major antiphagocytic virulence mechanism.
explanations.C: Incorrect (true statement). Both Gram-negative rods and Gram-negative cocci carry lipopolysaccharide endotoxin in their cell wall -- this is a property of the Gram-negative wall generally, not restricted to one particular bacterial shape.
explanations.D: Correct. This is the false statement, so it is the EXCEPT answer. Bacterial flagella are, in fact, strongly antigenic -- their flagellin protein is recognised by the host as the flagellar (H) antigen, used in serotyping organisms such as Salmonella and E. coli. They are also not chemically similar to any human structure: human cells carry no flagellum built from bacterial-type flagellin, so there is no structural basis for the claim that flagella are "nonantigenic in humans because they resemble human flagella."

questions.learning_objective: Identify that bacterial flagella ARE antigenic (the H antigen) and unrelated to any human structure, while correctly retaining pili-mediated adherence, capsule antiphagocytic function and Gram-negative LPS/endotoxin as true statements.

questions.title: Peptidoglycan structure: what's true, and what isn't (thickness)
questions.question: Each of the following statements concerning peptidoglycan is correct EXCEPT?

options.A: It has a backbone composed of alternating units of muramic acid and acetylglucosamine
options.B: Cross-links between the tetrapeptides involve d-alanine
options.C: It is thinner in gram-positive than in gram-negative cells
options.D: It can be degraded by lysozyme

explanations.A: Incorrect (true statement). The peptidoglycan backbone is indeed built from alternating N-acetylmuramic acid and N-acetylglucosamine sugar units.
explanations.B: Incorrect (true statement). The peptide cross-links between adjacent peptidoglycan strands do involve a D-alanine residue at the terminus of the pentapeptide side chain.
explanations.C: Correct. This is the false statement, so it is the EXCEPT answer. Peptidoglycan is, in fact, much THICKER in Gram-positive bacteria than in Gram-negative bacteria -- the reverse of what this statement claims. This thickness difference is exactly what makes Gram-positive walls retain the crystal violet stain (thick mesh traps the dye complex) while Gram-negative walls, with only a thin peptidoglycan layer, let the stain wash out.
explanations.D: Incorrect (true statement). Lysozyme does degrade peptidoglycan, cleaving the beta-1,4 glycosidic bond between its alternating sugar units -- this is the basis of protoplast/spheroplast formation when bacteria are treated with lysozyme.

questions.learning_objective: State that peptidoglycan's alternating-sugar backbone, D-alanine cross-links and lysozyme susceptibility are all correct, while its thickness is greater (not thinner) in Gram-positive than Gram-negative walls.

questions.title: Mycoplasma: the one prokaryote with membrane sterol
questions.question: Sterol is not a constituent of cytoplasmic membrane of all prokaryotes EXCEPT?

explanations.A: Incorrect. E. coli, like almost every other bacterium, lacks sterol in its cytoplasmic membrane.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Staphylococcus aureus's membrane, like other typical bacteria, contains no sterol.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Chlamydia is an obligate intracellular bacterium but does not have a sterol-containing membrane; it lacks classical peptidoglycan for a different reason (a distinct cell-wall biology), not a sterol-containing membrane.
explanations.D: Correct. Mycoplasma is the singular exception among bacteria: its cytoplasmic membrane contains cholesterol, a sterol scavenged from the host cell, which stabilises the membrane in the permanent absence of a peptidoglycan cell wall. Every other listed organism follows the general prokaryotic rule of a sterol-free membrane; Mycoplasma alone breaks it, which is also why its membrane needs this extra structural support -- it has no rigid wall to rely on instead.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Klebsiella, an ordinary Gram-negative rod, has no sterol in its cytoplasmic membrane.

questions.learning_objective: Identify Mycoplasma as the one bacterial genus whose cytoplasmic membrane contains sterol (cholesterol), unlike E. coli, S. aureus, Chlamydia or Klebsiella.

questions.title: Bacterial respiratory enzymes reside in the cytoplasmic membrane
questions.question: Respiratory activities in human cells are associated with mitochondria while in bacteria they are associated with?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Flagella are the motility organelle; they play no role in cellular respiration.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The capsule is an antiphagocytic/adherence structure external to the cell wall; it has no respiratory function.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Pili mediate adherence (or, as sex pili, conjugation); they play no role in respiration.
explanations.D: Correct. Bacteria have no mitochondria, so the respiratory (electron transport chain) enzymes that a eukaryotic cell houses in its mitochondria are instead located in the bacterial cytoplasmic membrane -- classically at membrane invaginations called mesosomes. This substitution of the cytoplasmic membrane for a dedicated respiratory organelle is a direct consequence of the prokaryotic cell's lack of membrane-bound organelles altogether. It is a key structural/functional distinction tested repeatedly in comparing prokaryotic to eukaryotic cell biology.
explanations.E: Incorrect. The cell wall provides shape and rigidity and is a site of action for some antibiotics; it has no respiratory enzyme function.

questions.learning_objective: State that bacterial respiratory enzymes are housed in the cytoplasmic membrane (at mesosomes), replacing the mitochondrion's role, since bacteria have no mitochondria.

questions.title: Peptidoglycan maintains bacterial rigidity and shape
questions.question: The bacterial structure that maintains rigidity and shape of the cell is?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Teichoic acid is a Gram-positive wall component that contributes to wall charge and immune activation; it does not itself provide structural rigidity.
explanations.B: Correct. Peptidoglycan (murein) -- a mesh-like sacculus of alternating sugar chains cross-linked by short peptides -- is the structural component that gives the bacterial cell wall its rigidity and characteristic shape, and lets it resist osmotic lysis. Removing peptidoglycan (e.g. with lysozyme) is exactly what causes a bacterium to lose its normal shape and become a rounded protoplast or spheroplast, which is direct evidence that peptidoglycan -- not any of the other listed molecules -- is responsible for shape and rigidity.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Lipopolysaccharide is the Gram-negative outer-membrane component responsible for endotoxin activity, not structural rigidity.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Capsular polysaccharide forms the antiphagocytic capsule outside the wall; it does not provide the wall's structural rigidity.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Lipid A is the toxic lipid moiety of LPS responsible for endotoxin activity, not a structural/rigidity component.

questions.learning_objective: Identify peptidoglycan as the wall component responsible for bacterial rigidity and shape, distinct from teichoic acid, LPS, capsular polysaccharide and Lipid A.

questions.title: Lipid A is the toxic moiety of endotoxin
questions.question: The toxicity of gram-negative bacteria endotoxin is due to the presence of?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Peptidoglycan gives the wall its rigidity; it is not the toxic component of endotoxin.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The polysaccharide portion of LPS (the O antigen and core polysaccharide) is mainly antigenic/structural, not the toxic moiety itself.
explanations.C: Correct. Endotoxin's toxicity resides specifically in Lipid A, the lipid anchor of lipopolysaccharide embedded in the Gram-negative outer membrane -- it is Lipid A that triggers the host inflammatory cascade (fever, hypotension, disseminated intravascular coagulation in severe cases) when released, typically on bacterial lysis. This is why endotoxin activity tracks with Lipid A specifically, rather than with the polysaccharide chains attached to it, which mainly determine antigenic specificity (serotype) rather than toxicity.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The periplasmic space is the compartment between the inner and outer membranes holding transport/hydrolytic proteins; it is not itself a toxic component.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Teichoic acid is a Gram-positive wall component and is not present in the Gram-negative wall at all, let alone responsible for endotoxin toxicity.

questions.learning_objective: Identify Lipid A as the specific toxic component of Gram-negative endotoxin (lipopolysaccharide), not the polysaccharide chains, periplasmic space or teichoic acid.

questions.title: Cell wall determines staining affinity
questions.question: The bacterial structure responsible for staining affinity is?

explanations.A: Incorrect. The cytoplasmic membrane lies beneath the wall and is not what determines whether a cell retains or loses the crystal violet stain.
explanations.B: Correct. Staining affinity in the Gram stain procedure is determined by the cell wall -- specifically, by how much peptidoglycan the wall contains and whether it is exposed to (Gram-positive, thick wall retains stain) or shielded by an outer membrane from (Gram-negative, thin wall loses stain) the decolourising step. This is the same underlying wall-thickness mechanism that produces the violet-vs-pink colour difference, so the cell wall -- not the membrane, Lipid A, mesosomes or endotoxin -- is the structure "responsible" for staining affinity.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Lipid A is the toxic moiety of LPS; it plays no role in the mechanics of Gram staining.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Mesosomes are membrane invaginations with a respiratory role; they are not the structure responsible for stain retention.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Endotoxin (LPS) is a Gram-negative outer-membrane component with a toxic function; it does not determine Gram-stain colour, which depends on the peptidoglycan wall.

questions.learning_objective: Identify the cell wall (its peptidoglycan thickness) as the structure responsible for Gram-stain affinity.

questions.title: Mycoplasma is naturally resistant to penicillin (no cell wall to target)
questions.question: All the following are characters of mycoplasma EXCEPT?

explanations.A: Incorrect (true statement). Mycoplasma is pleomorphic -- lacking a rigid peptidoglycan wall, it has no fixed shape.
explanations.B: Incorrect (true statement). Mycoplasma is genetically incapable of synthesising peptidoglycan and so is permanently wall-less.
explanations.C: Correct. This is the false statement, so it is the EXCEPT answer. Because penicillin (and other beta-lactams) work by blocking peptidoglycan cross-linking, an organism with no peptidoglycan wall at all -- Mycoplasma -- has no target for the drug and is therefore intrinsically resistant to penicillin, not sensitive to it. This is a direct, mechanistic consequence of Mycoplasma's permanent wall-lessness, unlike an induced L-form, whose wall loss is caused by an agent such as a beta-lactam antibiotic in the first place.
explanations.D: Incorrect (true statement). Having no peptidoglycan wall to retain or lose the crystal violet stain, Mycoplasma does not take up the Gram stain in the usual sense.
explanations.E: Incorrect (true statement). Mycoplasma's cytoplasmic membrane uniquely contains sterol (cholesterol), which helps stabilise it in the absence of a wall.

questions.learning_objective: Identify that Mycoplasma, being permanently wall-less, is intrinsically RESISTANT to penicillin (not sensitive), while correctly being pleomorphic, wall-less, Gram-stain-negative and sterol-membraned.

questions.title: What the bacterial capsule does NOT do: form outside the host exclusively
questions.question: Bacterial capsule has the following characters EXCEPT?

explanations.A: Incorrect (true statement). The capsule is mostly polysaccharide in composition (polypeptide only in the Bacillus anthracis exception).
explanations.B: Incorrect (true statement). Antiphagocytic activity -- resisting engulfment by host phagocytes -- is the capsule's defining virulence function.
explanations.C: Incorrect (true statement). The capsule does not take up the Gram stain in the usual sense and typically appears as a clear halo around the cell on special capsule stains.
explanations.D: Correct. This is the false statement, so it is the EXCEPT answer. Capsule formation is not restricted to outside the host -- many encapsulated pathogens form or even upregulate their capsule while established inside a host, since the antiphagocytic advantage the capsule confers is most valuable precisely during an in-host infection, not only in the external environment.
explanations.E: Incorrect (true statement). The capsule's antigenic specificity makes it immunogenic, which is exactly what underlies capsular serotyping and capsular-polysaccharide vaccines.

questions.learning_objective: Identify that capsule formation is not restricted to outside the host, while correctly recognising the capsule as mostly polysaccharide, antiphagocytic, Gram-stain-negative and immunogenic.

field_notes.keySource: printed plain-text ANSWERS table, chapter 1, p26

questions.title: Bacillus anthracis: the polypeptide-capsule exception
questions.question: The capsule of the following organisms is polysaccharide in composition EXCEPT?

explanations.A: Incorrect (true statement). Haemophilus influenzae's capsule (e.g. the type b polyribosylribitol phosphate capsule) is polysaccharide.
explanations.B: Incorrect (true statement). The pneumococcal capsule, the basis of pneumococcal serotyping and vaccines, is polysaccharide.
explanations.C: Correct. This is the exception, so it is the EXCEPT answer. Bacillus anthracis is the classic exception to the rule that bacterial capsules are polysaccharide -- its capsule is instead composed of poly-D-glutamic acid, a polypeptide, unlike every other organism listed here.
explanations.D: Incorrect (true statement). The meningococcal capsule is polysaccharide, and is the basis of meningococcal vaccines.
explanations.E: Incorrect (true statement). Klebsiella's prominent capsule is polysaccharide in composition.

questions.learning_objective: Identify Bacillus anthracis as the exception whose capsule is polypeptide (poly-D-glutamic acid), not polysaccharide like H. influenzae, pneumococci, meningococci and Klebsiella.

questions.title: Bacterial ribosomes assemble into polysomes
questions.question: Which of the following is CORRECT regarding bacterial ribosomes?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Bacterial ribosomes are 70S, not 80S -- 80S is the eukaryotic cytoplasmic ribosome size.
explanations.B: Correct. During active protein synthesis, several bacterial ribosomes attach simultaneously to one messenger RNA strand, forming a polysome (polyribosome) -- this increases translation throughput from a single mRNA transcript. This polysome-forming behaviour, together with being 70S rather than 80S, is a standard testable feature of bacterial ribosomes.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Bacterial respiration takes place at the cytoplasmic membrane (classically at mesosomes), not at the ribosome, which is the site of protein synthesis.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Ribosome-targeting antibiotics include aminoglycosides, macrolides and tetracyclines, which exploit the 70S-vs-80S size difference -- penicillin instead targets peptidoglycan cross-linking in the cell wall, not the ribosome.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Staining affinity in the Gram stain depends on the cell wall's peptidoglycan content, not on the ribosome.

questions.learning_objective: State that bacterial (70S) ribosomes assemble into polysomes during active translation, and reject the false claims about size, respiration, penicillin sensitivity and staining affinity.

questions.title: Lysozyme causes bacteria to lose their normal shape
questions.question: Bacteria treated with lysozyme will?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Lysozyme degrades peptidoglycan in the wall; it does not directly disturb the respiratory enzymes, which sit in the cytoplasmic membrane.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Selective permeability is a property of the cytoplasmic membrane, which lysozyme does not directly act on -- lysozyme's target is the peptidoglycan wall, external to the membrane.
explanations.C: Correct. Lysozyme cleaves the beta-1,4 glycosidic bonds of peptidoglycan, degrading the rigid wall that normally maintains the bacterium's characteristic shape. With that structural support gone, the cell loses its normal shape and rounds up -- becoming a wall-less protoplast (from a Gram-positive cell) or a spheroplast (from a Gram-negative cell, which retains a residual outer-membrane layer) if kept in an osmotically protective medium, or lysing outright if not.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Lysozyme is an enzyme that digests peptidoglycan; it has no mutagenic effect on bacterial DNA.

questions.learning_objective: State that lysozyme's degradation of peptidoglycan causes bacteria to lose their normal shape, connecting this to protoplast/spheroplast formation.

field_notes.keySource: printed plain-text ANSWERS table, chapter 1, p26

questions.title: The outer membrane is absent from Gram-positive bacteria
questions.question: Which of the following structure is NOT found in gram positive bacterin?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Gram-positive bacteria do have a cell wall -- a thick peptidoglycan one.
explanations.B: Correct. The outer membrane (carrying LPS, enclosing a periplasmic space) is specifically a Gram-negative structure. Gram-positive bacteria have no outer membrane at all -- their wall is just a thick peptidoglycan mesh with embedded teichoic acid, external to the cytoplasmic membrane, with nothing further out. This is exactly the structural feature that, alongside peptidoglycan thickness, distinguishes the two Gram types.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Peptidoglycan is present in Gram-positive bacteria, and in fact thicker than in Gram-negative bacteria.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Teichoic acid is a Gram-positive-specific wall component, present in Gram-positive but absent from Gram-negative bacteria.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Ribosomes (70S) are present in all bacteria, Gram-positive included -- they are not a Gram-type-specific structure.

questions.learning_objective: Identify the outer membrane as the structure absent from Gram-positive bacteria, distinguishing it from the (present) cell wall, peptidoglycan, teichoic acid and ribosomes.

field_notes.keySource: printed plain-text ANSWERS table, chapter 1, p26

questions.title: The cytoplasmic membrane is present in prokaryotes
questions.question: Which of the following is present in prokaryotes?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Prokaryotes have 70S ribosomes, not the eukaryotic 80S.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Prokaryotes have no mitochondria at all.
explanations.C: Correct. Every prokaryotic cell has a cytoplasmic (plasma) membrane -- the selectively permeable barrier enclosing the cytoplasm, and (since there is no mitochondrion) also the site of respiratory enzyme activity. This is the one genuinely present feature among the options, each of the others being a specifically eukaryotic feature the prokaryotic cell lacks.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Prokaryotes have no nucleolus, a substructure of the eukaryotic nucleus, which prokaryotes also lack.
explanations.E: Incorrect. A prokaryote typically has a single chromosome, not multiple -- multiple linear chromosomes are the eukaryotic pattern.

questions.learning_objective: Identify the cytoplasmic membrane as present in prokaryotes, rejecting the eukaryote-only features 80S ribosomes, mitochondria, nucleolus and multiple chromosomes.

field_notes.keySource: printed plain-text ANSWERS table, chapter 1, p26

questions.title: The cell wall plays no role in cell respiration
questions.question: All of the following is true regarding bacterial cell wall EXCEPT?

options.A: Plays a role in cell division
options.B: Plays a role in cell respiration
options.D: Maintains the shape of the bacteria

explanations.A: Incorrect (true statement). The cell wall is involved in cell division via septum formation at the division site.
explanations.B: Correct. This is the false statement, so it is the EXCEPT answer. Cellular respiration in bacteria occurs at the cytoplasmic membrane (classically its mesosome invaginations), not the cell wall -- the wall's roles are structural (shape, rigidity, division, antigenicity, staining), not respiratory.
explanations.C: Incorrect (true statement). The Gram-negative wall's LPS functions as the somatic (O) antigen, used in serotyping.
explanations.D: Incorrect (true statement). The rigid peptidoglycan mesh of the wall maintains the bacterium's characteristic shape.
explanations.E: Incorrect (true statement). The wall's peptidoglycan content determines Gram-stain affinity/retention.

questions.learning_objective: Identify that the cell wall plays no role in cell respiration (a cytoplasmic-membrane function), while correctly crediting it with roles in division, somatic antigenicity, shape and staining affinity.

field_notes.keySource: printed plain-text ANSWERS table, chapter 1, p26

questions.title: Penicillin can induce bacterial L-forms
questions.question: L-forms of bacteria are likely if the following antibiotic is present in the culture?

explanations.A: Correct. L-forms are cell-wall-deficient bacterial variants that arise when a wall-active agent -- classically a beta-lactam antibiotic such as penicillin -- blocks peptidoglycan synthesis in an otherwise wall-forming species, in an osmotically protective environment. Unlike Mycoplasma's permanent, genetically determined wall-lessness, an L-form's wall loss is induced, and the underlying organism retains the genetic capacity to make a wall again once the inducing agent is removed.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Erythromycin (a macrolide) inhibits protein synthesis at the 50S ribosomal subunit; it does not act on the cell wall and does not typically induce L-forms.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Streptomycin (an aminoglycoside) inhibits protein synthesis at the 30S ribosomal subunit; it is not a wall-active agent.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Tetracycline inhibits protein synthesis at the 30S ribosomal subunit; it is not a wall-active agent and does not classically induce L-forms.

questions.learning_objective: Identify penicillin (a wall-active beta-lactam) as the antibiotic classically capable of inducing bacterial L-forms, unlike the protein-synthesis inhibitors erythromycin, streptomycin and tetracycline.

field_notes.keySource: printed plain-text ANSWERS table, chapter 1, p26

questions.title: The capsule helps type (serotype) bacterial species
questions.question: Which of the following is CORRECT regarding bacterial capsule?

options.D: Helps in typing certain bacterial species

explanations.A: Incorrect. Capsule formation is not restricted to outside the host; many organisms form or upregulate their capsule while established inside a host, where its antiphagocytic advantage matters most.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Surviving unfavourable environmental conditions over the long term is the endospore's role, not the capsule's -- the capsule's role is chiefly antiphagocytic, aiding survival against the host immune system during active infection.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The capsule is mostly polysaccharide (polypeptide only in the Bacillus anthracis exception), not lipid, in composition.
explanations.D: Correct. Each capsular type has a distinct antigenic structure, and this antigenic specificity is used to identify and serotype (type) certain bacterial species -- for example, the many pneumococcal or meningococcal capsular serotypes. That same specificity is also the basis for capsular-polysaccharide vaccines, which target one or more particular serotypes. This typing/vaccine role is the one genuinely correct statement among the options offered here.
explanations.E: Incorrect. The capsule is, in fact, a major virulence factor (via its antiphagocytic action), not something inessential to virulence.

questions.learning_objective: Identify that the bacterial capsule's antigenic specificity is used to type (serotype) certain bacterial species, rejecting false claims about exclusive extra-host formation, protection from unfavourable conditions, lipid composition, and non-essentiality to virulence.

field_notes.keySource: printed plain-text ANSWERS table, chapter 1, p26

questions.title: Endotoxin is a component of the Gram-negative cell wall
questions.question: Endotoxin of bacteria is a component of?

explanations.A: Correct. Endotoxin is lipopolysaccharide (LPS), embedded in the outer membrane that is itself part of the Gram-negative cell wall. So endotoxin is, structurally, a component of the Gram-negative cell wall specifically. It is released mainly when the cell lyses, rather than being actively secreted the way an exotoxin is.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The capsule is a separate, outer structure (external to the wall) with an antiphagocytic function; it is not the endotoxin-bearing structure.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The cytoplasmic (cell) membrane lies internal to the wall and does not carry LPS/endotoxin.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Gram-positive bacteria have no outer membrane and therefore no LPS/endotoxin in their cell wall at all -- endotoxin is specifically a Gram-negative feature.
explanations.E: Incorrect. The periplasmic space is the compartment between the inner and outer membranes holding transport/hydrolytic proteins; it is not itself the endotoxin-bearing structure.

questions.learning_objective: State that endotoxin (LPS) is a component of the Gram-negative cell wall specifically, not the capsule, cell membrane, Gram-positive wall or periplasmic space.

questions.title: Pili: conjugation (sex pili) and adherence (ordinary pili)
questions.question: Pili can have two functions?

options.D: Nutrient uptake and protection from phagocytosis

explanations.A: Incorrect. Nutrient uptake and storage are not established pilus functions -- nutrient storage is instead the role of cytoplasmic inclusion granules.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Nutrient uptake is not an established pilus function, and "typing" (serotyping) is more classically a capsule-antigen-based property, not a pilus function.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Motility is the flagellum's job, not the pilus's -- pili do not confer motility.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Protection from phagocytosis is the capsule's antiphagocytic role, not a pilus function; nutrient uptake is likewise not an established pilus function.
explanations.E: Correct. Pili have two genuine, well-established functions: ordinary (common) pili mediate adherence of the bacterium to host cells and surfaces, the first step in many infections, while the specialised sex pilus mediates conjugation -- the transfer of DNA (e.g. a resistance plasmid) between two bacterial cells. Neither of the other listed pairings (nutrient uptake combined with storage, typing, motility or antiphagocytic protection) describes an actual pilus function.

questions.learning_objective: State that pili have two genuine functions -- adherence (ordinary pili) and conjugation (sex pili) -- rejecting distractor pairings involving nutrient uptake, typing, motility or antiphagocytic protection.

questions.title: Bacterial flagella are protein in nature
questions.question: The following characterizes bacterial flagella?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Flagella are long, thin and helical/flexible appendages driven by a rotary basal-body motor, not short and rigid structures.
explanations.B: Correct. The bacterial flagellum is a helical filament built from repeating subunits of the protein flagellin, rotated by a basal-body motor to drive the cell through liquid. Being built of protein, rather than a lipid or carbohydrate structure, is also exactly what makes it antigenic -- recognised by the host as the flagellar (H) antigen. This protein composition is the fact this question is testing, distinct from the flagellum's shape, chemical class, or role in adherence.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Lipopolysaccharide is a component of the Gram-negative outer membrane, unrelated to flagellar composition, which is protein (flagellin).
explanations.D: Incorrect. Adherence to host cells is mediated by pili, not flagella -- the flagellum's role is motility, not attachment.

questions.learning_objective: State that bacterial flagella are protein (flagellin) in nature, not short/rigid or lipopolysaccharide-based, and distinguish their motility role from the pilus's adherence role.

questions.title: Bacterial capsule is associated with virulence
questions.question: It is true for bacteria that?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Bacteria lack a true, membrane-bound nucleus -- their DNA sits in the unbound nucleoid region instead.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Adhesion to host cells is mediated by pili, not flagella -- flagella instead drive motility.
explanations.C: Correct. The capsule is a major virulence factor: its antiphagocytic action lets an encapsulated organism resist engulfment by host phagocytes, directly aiding the establishment of infection. This is a standard, high-yield association tested repeatedly across this bank -- capsule with virulence, distinct from the false pairings offered here (true nucleus, flagella-mediated adhesion, absent cell wall).
explanations.D: Incorrect. Most bacteria (Mycoplasma being the exception) do have a cell wall.

questions.learning_objective: State that the bacterial capsule is associated with virulence (via its antiphagocytic action), while rejecting false claims about a true nucleus, flagella-mediated adhesion, and absent cell wall.

questions.title: Normal flora is best termed commensals
questions.question: Normal flora is best called?

explanations.A: Incorrect. "Invasive" describes an organism that actively penetrates host tissue -- not the relationship of a normal, harmlessly-resident flora member.
explanations.B: Correct. Normal flora is best termed commensals -- organisms that benefit from residing on or in a healthy host while the host is neither helped nor harmed under ordinary circumstances. This is distinct from a saprophyte (which lives on dead/organic matter in the environment, not on a living host), an invasive organism (which actively penetrates tissue) and a true pathogen (whose normal behaviour is to cause disease).
explanations.C: Incorrect. "Saprophytic" describes an organism living on dead or decaying organic matter in the environment, not one residing on a living host.
explanations.D: Incorrect. A "true pathogen" causes disease as its ordinary behaviour -- the opposite of the harmless relationship normal flora has with a healthy host.

questions.learning_objective: Name "commensals" as the term for a healthy host's normal flora, distinguishing it from invasive, saprophytic and true-pathogen relationships.
